I’ll verify the four supplied sources only, then synthesize a traceable report.# HyperFund / HyperVerse Research Report

## Scope and Evidentiary Standard

This report uses only the four supplied sources: SRC-001 through SRC-004. It does not rely on benchmark catalogs, external databases, unsupported assumptions, or unverified identity claims. Allegations in charging documents and regulatory complaints are treated as allegations, not as final adjudicated facts. The DOJ expressly states that an indictment is merely an allegation and that defendants are presumed innocent. [2] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The strongest traceable evidence comes from the DOJ case page, the SEC press release, and The Guardian’s investigation. SRC-001 remains part of the supplied source set, but no material proposition in this report depends solely on a fact that cannot be independently anchored to the other supplied materials.

## Executive Finding

The supplied evidence supports a model in which the alleged operation combined:

1. **Investment memberships promising unusually high returns**;
2. **A mining-based explanation for those returns**;
3. **Regulatory allegations that investor funds, rather than genuine mining revenue, supplied the scheme’s real revenue**;
4. **Public promotion by identifiable individuals, including Sam Lee, Brenda Chunga, and Rodney Burton**;
5. **A multi-level referral structure that rewarded recruitment and re-recruitment**;
6. **Brand changes from HyperFund to HyperVerse and then HyperNation**; and
7. **A public-facing CEO persona, Steven Reece Lewis, whose stated credentials could not be independently verified by The Guardian.**

The evidence supports continuity at the level of branding, promotion, membership products, and participant migration. It does not conclusively establish that HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation were identical legal entities, nor does it provide a complete accounting of individual investor funds or a wallet-by-wallet reconstruction of payments.

## 1. Alleged Investment and Recruitment Mechanics

### Memberships, Returns, and Reinvestment

The DOJ states that, from June 2020 through November 2022, Sam Lee and co-conspirators allegedly offered and sold investment contracts to the public through HyperFund’s online platform. Promotional materials allegedly represented that investors who purchased HyperFund “memberships” would receive between 0.5% and 1% in daily passive rewards until their initial investment doubled or tripled. [2] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The Guardian describes a similar structure in more operational terms. It reports that the minimum membership amount was $300, that the investment was converted into HyperUnits, and that members were offered a minimum return of 0.5% per day, described as a 300% return over 600 days. Members were also encouraged to reinvest earnings rather than withdraw them. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The two descriptions should not be forced into a single exact formula. The DOJ describes a range of 0.5% to 1% daily rewards and a doubling or tripling of the initial investment, while The Guardian describes a minimum 0.5% daily return and a 300% return over 600 days. The common, source-supported point is that the program allegedly promised high, structured returns tied to membership participation.

### Referral Commissions and Downline Expansion

The Guardian reports that members received HyperUnits for recruiting new members, with commissions determined by the number of recruits. Additional commissions were reportedly paid based on the number of people recruited by those recruits, extending down to 20 levels. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

This evidence supports an alleged multi-level recruitment mechanism:

- A prospective participant encountered promotional material or a public launch;
- The participant purchased a membership;
- The membership generated promised rewards or HyperUnits;
- The participant was encouraged to reinvest;
- The participant could earn additional rewards by recruiting others; and
- The participant’s compensation could extend through multiple levels of downstream recruitment.

That structure is consistent with the SEC’s characterization of HyperFund as an alleged crypto-asset pyramid scheme. The SEC states that Lee and Chunga promoted membership packages promising high returns and alleges that HyperFund had no real source of revenue other than funds received from investors. [4] ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Withdrawal Restrictions and Collapse

The DOJ alleges that HyperFund began blocking investor withdrawals in at least July 2021. [2] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases)) The SEC states that the scheme collapsed in 2022 and that investors were no longer able to make withdrawals. [4] ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The Guardian likewise reports that some early investors were able to profit or withdraw, while many later investors were unable to access their funds. It also reports that affected members were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The supplied sources therefore support a chronology in which promised rewards and recruitment incentives were followed by withdrawal problems and a transition to another Hyper-branded platform. They do not, however, establish the exact date on which every withdrawal was blocked, the percentage of investors affected, or the full amount lost by any individual participant.

## 2. Mining Revenue Claims Versus Investor-Fund Allegations

### What the Sources Support

The alleged mining narrative was central to the investment proposition. The DOJ states that HyperFund allegedly told investors that payments would be funded partly by revenue from large-scale crypto-mining operations, but that HyperFund did not have such operations. [2] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The SEC makes the allegation more directly. It states that Lee and Chunga promoted returns supposedly connected to crypto-asset mining and that, according to the SEC’s complaint, HyperFund had “no real source of revenue other than funds received from investors.” [4] ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

Taken together, SRC-002 and SRC-004 support the following carefully qualified conclusion:

> The DOJ and SEC allege that the mining explanation was not supported by genuine large-scale mining operations and that investor funds, rather than mining revenue, supplied the scheme’s real revenue.

That is the evidentiary basis for the “investor funds rather than mining revenue” component of CONTRA-001.

### What the Sources Do Not Prove

The four supplied sources do not provide:

- Blockchain wallet addresses;
- Bank-account records;
- Mining facility records;
- Hash-rate or equipment data;
- A transaction-level tracing of deposits and withdrawals;
- A complete investor-by-investor loss schedule; or
- An independently reconstructed cash-flow model.

Accordingly, the evidence supports a regulatory and prosecutorial allegation about the source of revenue, but not a complete forensic accounting conclusion based on the supplied URLs alone.

## 3. Public Promotion and the Recruitment Funnel

### Sam Lee / Xue Lee — ENT-001

The SEC identifies Xue Lee, also known as Sam Lee, as a person charged in connection with the alleged HyperFund scheme. It states that Lee and Brenda Chunga promoted HyperFund membership packages between June 2020 and early 2022. [4] ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ describes Sam Lee as the alleged co-founder of HyperFund and states that HyperFund was also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [2] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The Guardian presents Lee as a public-facing figure in the promotional structure. It reports that Lee spoke at the HyperVerse launch as chairman of the HyperTech group, while another individual, Ryan Xu, was introduced as the group’s founder. The Guardian also identifies Lee as an Australian entrepreneur associated with the earlier Blockchain Global business. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The supplied sources therefore support these roles for ENT-001:

- Alleged co-founder of HyperFund;
- Also identified as Sam Lee or Xue Lee;
- Public promoter or executive-level spokesperson in the Hyper-branded ecosystem;
- Presented at the HyperVerse launch as chairman of HyperTech; and
- One of the individuals whom the SEC alleges promoted membership packages.

The sources do not establish every corporate title Lee may have held, nor do they independently resolve his later denial of involvement in HyperNation.

### Brenda Chunga / Bitcoin Beautee — ENT-002

The SEC expressly identifies Brenda Chunga as also known as Bitcoin Beautee and alleges that she promoted HyperFund membership packages with Lee. [4] ([sec.gov](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ identifies Brenda Chunga as a promoter of HyperFund and states that she was charged in connection with the alleged scheme. The DOJ page also states that Chunga pleaded guilty. [2] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The supplied evidence supports the following for ENT-002:

- Brenda Chunga;
- Alias Bitcoin Beautee;
- Promoter of HyperFund;
- Participant in promoting membership packages with Lee; and
- Defendant in the criminal and SEC proceedings described by the supplied sources.

The canonical label includes the middle name “Indah,” but the supplied source text reviewed here does not independently reproduce that middle name. The source-supported form is therefore Brenda Chunga / Bitcoin Beautee.

### Rodney Burton / Bitcoin Rodney — ENT-003

The DOJ identifies Rodney Burton as a promoter of HyperFund and states that he was charged with conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money-transmitting business and operating an unlicensed money-transmitting business. [2] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The source page identifies him as Rodney Burton but does not reproduce the alias “Bitcoin Rodney.” That alias is retained here only as part of the canonical label supplied in the brief, not as an independently verified fact from SRC-002 through SRC-004.

The supplied sources support that Burton was:

- Identified as a HyperFund promoter;
- Connected to the public promotional side of the scheme; and
- Charged in relation to alleged unlicensed money-transmission activity.

The four sources do not provide a detailed record of Burton’s individual videos, speeches, social-media posts, compensation, or direct communications with specific investors. It would therefore be unsupported to attribute particular promotional statements to him without additional source evidence.

### The Public-to-Investor Funnel

The source record supports a multi-stage public recruitment funnel:

1. **Public narrative:** HyperFund and later HyperVerse were presented as crypto, blockchain, mining, or metaverse opportunities.
2. **Public spokespersons:** Lee, Chunga, Burton, and other promoters helped expose prospective participants to the opportunity.
3. **Executive credibility:** Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse’s CEO, with an impressive professional and academic biography.
4. **Social proof:** HyperVerse’s launch was accompanied by messages from public figures, including Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass.
5. **Call to action:** Reece Lewis encouraged people to become early supporters of HyperVerse.
6. **Paid entry:** Investors purchased memberships, reportedly beginning at $300.
7. **Return expectations:** Members were promised daily rewards and eventual multiples of their initial investment.
8. **Retention:** Members were encouraged to reinvest rather than withdraw.
9. **Network expansion:** Members received referral rewards for recruiting others, extending down multiple levels.
10. **Migration:** When withdrawal issues arose, some members were encouraged to move to HyperNation.

The Guardian states that the celebrity messages were released while HyperVerse was increasing its global recruitment effort. It also reports that there was no suggestion that the celebrities understood the business model or that their messages referred to money or investments. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

This distinction is important: the supplied sources support the existence of public promotional material and celebrity messages, but they do not establish that every person appearing in promotional content understood or endorsed the alleged investment mechanics.

## 4. Rebranding and Organizational Continuity

### Direct Evidence of Rebranding

The DOJ describes HyperFund as also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. [2] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases)) This is the clearest source-supported basis for treating ENT-004, ENT-005, and ENT-006 as connected names within the alleged operation.

The Guardian separately describes HyperVerse as linked to a previous scheme called HyperFund. It reports that, after members experienced withdrawal problems, some were encouraged to migrate to HyperNation. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

These sources support the following continuity proposition:

> The Hyper-branded names were presented and used within a connected promotional and membership ecosystem, with HyperVerse following HyperFund and HyperNation appearing as a later platform or entity associated with the same broader setup.

### Evidence Supporting a Shared Setup

The Guardian reports that a senior promoter described HyperVerse and HyperNation as “one big entity,” with HyperNation characterized as a new entity within the same setup. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

That statement is significant because it connects the names operationally from the perspective of a promoter and member community. It supports the inference that rebranding was not merely an unrelated change in subject matter. Instead, the same participant base appears to have been directed toward a new Hyper-branded platform after problems arose with the earlier one.

This is an inference from the combination of:

- The DOJ’s “also known as” formulation;
- The Guardian’s description of HyperVerse as linked to HyperFund;
- The reported migration from HyperVerse to HyperNation; and
- The promoter’s description of the brands as one big entity.

### Limits on the Continuity Claim

The supplied sources do not conclusively establish that HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation were the same legal entity. They do not provide:

- Corporate registration documents;
- Articles of incorporation;
- Ownership records;
- Common bank accounts;
- Common wallet addresses;
- Terms of service showing identical contracting entities; or
- A definitive legal analysis of whether the names represented aliases, subsidiaries, successors, or separate projects.

The Guardian also reports that Reece Lewis did not appear in the HyperNation launch video and was not referred to there. It further reports that Lee denied being involved in HyperNation and said he was not in a position to explain who “Mr H” was. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

Accordingly, the evidence supports continuity in branding, promotion, membership migration, and community structure, but it leaves the precise legal and ownership relationship unresolved.

## 5. Steven Reece Lewis — ENT-007

### Promotional Presentation

The Guardian reports that Steven Reece Lewis was introduced as HyperVerse’s chief executive officer at an online global launch event in December 2021. The promotional material described him as a University of Leeds graduate with a master’s degree from the University of Cambridge, and stated that he had worked for Goldman Sachs, sold a web-development company to Adobe, and launched an IT start-up before being recruited to lead HyperVerse. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The presentation also positioned Reece Lewis as a person whose leadership would help establish HyperVerse as a major metaverse project. The Guardian reports that he urged people to join as early supporters. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

This gave the alleged operation a conventional executive narrative: investors were not merely being asked to buy a speculative token or membership; they were being shown a purported CEO with elite academic, corporate, and entrepreneurial credentials.

### Verification Problems

The Guardian reports that it could not verify the qualifications and career history attributed to Reece Lewis. Specifically, it states that:

- The University of Leeds and University of Cambridge had no record of him under that name;
- No record was found on the UK Companies House register;
- No record was found in SEC materials;
- Adobe had no record in its public SEC filings of acquiring a company owned by him;
- Goldman Sachs could not find a record of his employment;
- No LinkedIn profile or broader internet presence was found beyond HyperVerse promotional material; and
- A Twitter account in his name appeared shortly before the launch and was used to promote HyperVerse for approximately six months.

The Guardian states that his identity could not be verified and that he could not be contacted for comment. [3] ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The source-supported conclusion is therefore that Reece Lewis was **presented as a CEO with an impressive biography, but that biography and identity could not be independently verified by the investigation**. The evidence supports describing the persona as questionable, unsubstantiated, or unverified. It does not, by itself, establish every detail of who created the persona or conclusively prove the existence or nonexistence of a person with that name.

### Relationship to SEC and DOJ Allegations

CONTRA-001 combines two related but distinct propositions:

1. Promotional materials presented Steven Reece Lewis as CEO; and
2. SEC and DOJ materials alleged a false or unsubstantiated executive identity while also alleging reliance on investor funds rather than mining revenue.

The supplied SEC and DOJ pages support the second part concerning alleged reliance on investor funds rather than mining revenue. [2] [4] ([justice.gov](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

However, the specific accessible DOJ and SEC pages reviewed here do not themselves name Steven Reece Lewis or expressly allege that his identity was false. That component is supported by The Guardian’s independent verification failures, not by a direct SEC or DOJ statement in the supplied pages. The contradiction should therefore be stated narrowly and accurately: **the promotional presentation of Reece Lewis as CEO conflicts with the inability of The Guardian to verify his claimed credentials and institutional history; the SEC and DOJ separately allege that the operation lacked genuine mining revenue and depended on investor funds.**

## 6. Traceable Claims and Evidentiary Limits

### Claims Supported by the Supplied Sources

The supplied sources support the following claims, subject to allegation and attribution language:

- HyperFund allegedly sold memberships or investment contracts promising high daily returns.
- The operation allegedly attributed those returns partly to crypto-mining revenue.
- The DOJ and SEC allege that genuine large-scale mining operations or other real revenue sources did not support the promised payments.
- The SEC alleges that investor funds were the real source of revenue.
- Sam Lee was identified as an alleged co-founder and promoter.
- Brenda Chunga, also known as Bitcoin Beautee, was identified as a promoter.
- Rodney Burton was identified as a promoter, although the alias Bitcoin Rodney is not reproduced in the source text reviewed here.
- HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation were presented as connected names or entities within the same broader setup.
- Members were reportedly encouraged to migrate from HyperVerse to HyperNation after withdrawal problems.
- Steven Reece Lewis was presented as HyperVerse CEO, but his claimed credentials could not be independently verified by The Guardian.
- The recruitment system allegedly used referral commissions and multi-level downline incentives.

### Claims That Must Be Omitted or Qualified

The supplied sources do not establish, without further evidence:

- That every Hyper-branded entity was legally identical;
- That every public promoter knew the alleged business model was fraudulent;
- That every celebrity endorsement represented informed support for an investment product;
- That Steven Reece Lewis was definitively fictional rather than merely unverified;
- That Burton personally made specific statements not reproduced in the supplied sources;
- That all investor funds were diverted in the same manner;
- The precise allocation of funds among mining, promotion, withdrawals, operating expenses, or personal use; or
- A complete list of victims, investor losses, or promoter commissions.

## Overall Conclusion

Based exclusively on the supplied evidence, the alleged operation appears to have combined a high-return membership proposition, a mining-based explanation, and a layered recruitment system with a strong public-relations presentation. The membership product allegedly promised daily rewards and encouraged reinvestment, while referral commissions created incentives for participants to recruit additional members and extend the network through multiple levels.

Sam Lee is supported as an alleged co-founder and senior public figure; Brenda Chunga is supported as a promoter using the alias Bitcoin Beautee; and Rodney Burton is supported as a promoter, although the supplied sources do not independently reproduce the alias Bitcoin Rodney. HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation are connected by the DOJ’s “also known as” formulation and by evidence of participant migration and shared promotional infrastructure, but the sources do not conclusively establish their exact legal relationship.

Steven Reece Lewis functioned as a credibility device within the promotional funnel: he was presented as a qualified CEO, encouraged early participation, and was supported by celebrity messages. The Guardian’s inability to verify his stated background creates a serious provenance problem. That issue should be kept analytically separate from the SEC and DOJ allegations about mining revenue and investor funds, because the supplied SEC and DOJ pages support the latter more directly than the former.
